newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein must make next N.Irish peace move - Mowlam.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein must make next N.Irish peace move - Mowlam.

text.p: Britain's new minister for Northern Ireland challenged the IRA's political wing on Saturday to restart stalled peace talks by persuading the guerrillas to declare a new ceasefire.
Marjorie Mowlam threw down the gauntlet on a visit to Belfast just hours after being appointed by new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair.

Before she was named to the post, Mowlam made clear that the Irish Republican Army had to call a credible ceasefire before its political arm, Sinn Fein, would be allowed to join multi-party peace talks.
The previous Conservative government adopted the same position.

"What I have said now is that the ball is in Sinn Fein's court. That is where the process needs to be taken and that's the only way we can know we have a position where the inclusive talks we would like to see are possible," she said.
In Thursday's general election, Sinn Fein won two of Northern Ireland's 18 seats in the British parliament, marking its biggest political advance for 40 years.
"In relation to the peace process, which is what I am interested in, the ball is still in their (Sinn Fein's) court. The walls haven't shifted," Mowlam said.

Earlier, Irish Deputy Prime Minister Dick Sping called on all sides in Northern Ireland's sectarian conflict to step up peace efforts, and said the Dublin government was ready to work closely with Blair.
He urged Gerry Adams and Martin McGuinness, the two victorious Sinn Fein election candidates, to press their IRA allies for an end to violence.
"There is...a huge onus on the newly-elected MPs. We must have a stop to the violence, we must get them into discussions," Spring said.
"But the first requirement for everybody now -- and there's some hope, I believe, today -- is to have a ceasefire and to allow everybody into talks."
He said his government wanted a meeting with Blair next week to get to grips with "paramilitary violence, confrontational marches, church burnings, sectarian tensions and political intransigence".

More than 3,000 people have died over the last 30 years in Northern Ireland in fighting between Protestants who want to stay part of Britain and Catholics who want the region to be united with Ireland.
The IRA, fighting to end British rule, abandoned a previous 17-month truce in February last year after accusing then prime minister John Major of blocking attempts to ensure a lasting peace.

Mowlam, who recently disclosed she underwent treatment earlier this year for a benign brain tumour, was enthusiasticaly greeted by afternoon shoppers when she went on a "walkaround" in a busy Belfast shopping area.
"My first priority is to come here and listen to people in Northern Ireland and be as open and responsive as I can," she told reporters.
Asked if she felt physically capable of tackling the onerous job, Mowlam replied: "My health is fine...and there is absolutely no problem."
She added: "It would be very naive to suggest that I can find solutions to problems very quickly but I think there is a sensitivity that needs to be shown and I will do my best to do that.
"I hope it is one of the advantages I might bring to the job."
Irish newspapers said the election of Adams and McGuinness, and the landslide victory by Blair's Labour Party, strengthened hopes for a fresh IRA ceasefire.
"The coming weeks could prove crucial in laying the basis for a restored ceasefire with confidence-building measures from both sides (Britain and the IRA)," said Dublin's Irish Times.

Belfast's daily nationalist newspaper, The Irish News, said that behind-the-scenes moves would soon be made "to bring key politial players back into action in Washington, London, Dublin and Belfast to try to rebuild the shattered peace process."
